suggestions.title: The two ketone strategies: what the choice decides, and what the salts do for the fog

edits.before: You must pick one of two ketone strategies, because the salts in one bring their own sodium while the diet in the other drains it. If you're in a crisis and need the fog gone fast, there's Strategy A, the "Crisis Mode". You drink BHB (beta-hydroxybutyrate) salts and keep eating a standard low-sugar diet.
edits.after: Your ketone strategy decides how you handle salt, since the salts bring their own sodium while the diet drains it. If you're in a crisis and need the fog to lift fast, there's Strategy A, the "Crisis Mode". You drink BHB (beta-hydroxybutyrate) salts and keep eating a standard low-sugar diet. In trials, ketone esters, salts and MCT oil improved thinking a little against a placebo, from a single dose as well as over two weeks or more (Bonnechère, et al, 2026).

suggestions.what: Block 95 no longer says you must pick one strategy: it says your strategy decides how you handle salt. "Need the fog gone fast" becomes "need the fog to lift fast", and a sentence gives what trials found ketone supplements do for thinking.
suggestions.why: Reading the protocol as a whole, block 95 says you must pick one strategy, but the timeline starts you on the salts, moves you to the diet in Weeks 3 to 5, and still has you "Drink BHB" when foggy on the diet. Your post said the choice "determines your electrolyte protocol", and that's what holds: one after the other, the two don't clash, and the salts' sodium on the diet just goes toward what the diet drains. The Oslo PTSD study, which measured ketosis three times a day, gave both together ([Edwards, et al, 2024](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39588043/)). On the fog, in a 2026 meta-analysis of 29 trial protocols (1,117 people), ketone esters, salts and MCT oil improved thinking a little against a placebo, about as much after a single dose as over two weeks or more, and more at higher daily doses ([Bonnechère, et al, 2026](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/42063954/)). Some found nothing, such as one in adults with type 2 diabetes ([Baranowski, et al, 2025](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39804761/)) and one in low oxygen ([Stalmans, et al, 2025](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40315254/)). So "gone" becomes "lift", with the size the trials found.
suggestions.stays: Strategy A, the "Crisis Mode", with the salts and a standard low-sugar diet; Strategy B below it; and the timeline as it is, starting on the salts, moving to the diet, the salts when foggy.
suggestions.deciding: Whether block 95 says what the choice of strategy decides, instead of that you must pick one, and gives what the salts do for thinking at the size trials found.
suggestions.advice_note: Approve. I'm sure of what the trials found. A fresh reader would drop the trials sentence as not needed to choose; I'd keep it, since the promise that the fog lifts is made as science and the reader learns how much to expect. That reader's version: "Your ketone strategy decides how you handle salt, since the salts bring their own sodium while the diet drains it. If you're in a crisis and need the fog to lift fast, there's Strategy A, the "Crisis Mode". You drink BHB (beta-hydroxybutyrate) salts and keep eating a standard low-sugar diet."

suggestions.title: DMSO in the Glutamate Shield, with your 1967 paper

inserts.text: DMSO (99.9%): Smell it, as in the Fog table below. In rat brain cells in a dish, DMSO at 0.5 to 1.5% quickly turned down the signals glutamate sends through its NMDA and AMPA receptors, and the calcium they let in. It also kept glutamate from killing the cells (Lu & Mattson, 2001). Back in 1967, doctors in Lima injected it into the muscles of 42 psychiatric inpatients, and nine of them had severe anxiety or obsessive-compulsive disorder. Within days they grew calmer, and the acute cases went home sooner than 16 patients with similar diagnoses who got the usual treatments of the time, such as electroshock, insulin comas and tranquilizers (Ramírez & Luza, 1967). There was no placebo, though, and the patients they were compared with weren't picked at random. In a second dish study, DMSO at 0.5% and 1% killed rat brain cells by itself, and injections of it set off widespread cell death in young mice's brains (Hanslick, et al, 2009). So if you're pregnant, don't use it, and keep it away from children. Nobody has measured how much reaches your brain when you smell it. And no trial has tested it for PTSD, so for PTSD it rests on what people report, and many say it helps.

suggestions.what: The DMSO item as before (smell it, as the Fog table says; your study's finding in a dish; the second dish study and young mice, so not in pregnancy or around children), now with your 1967 paper: nine people with severe anxiety or obsessive-compulsive disorder among 42 inpatients grew calmer within days on DMSO injections, with the study's limits. "No trial has tested it for anxiety or PTSD" becomes PTSD only.
suggestions.why: You were right to send it: my last card said no trial had tested DMSO for anxiety, and this one did, in 1967. Read in full: in Lima, 42 psychiatric inpatients (25 with schizophrenia, four in mania, four with alcoholic psychoses, four with obsessive-compulsive disorder and five with severe anxiety) got 50 to 80% DMSO injected into the muscle, one to five 5 ml vials a day. Agitation eased from the first doses, the anxious patients said they felt calm, and the acute cases left the hospital sooner than 16 patients with similar diagnoses on electroshock, insulin comas and the drugs of the day, about half as long for schizophrenia and the anxiety states in the paper's chart ([Ramírez & Luza, 1967](https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1749-6632.1967.tb34937.x)). Its limits go in with it: no placebo (they say its smell made blinding impossible), a comparison group not picked at random, barbiturates for the most agitated in the first days, and injections, not smelling. My search had asked for "psychiatric" with DMSO and read the newest hits, and a 1967 title says "mental patients"; that's the lesson this time. The rest of the item is as on the last card ([Lu & Mattson, 2001](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/11421595/); [Hanslick, et al, 2009](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19100327/); and in people, IV DMSO after head injury, [Huang & Wang, 2026](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/42939788/)).
suggestions.stays: Your safety note at the top, the Fog table and the timeline's "Inhale DMSO", as they are.
suggestions.deciding: Whether DMSO goes into the Glutamate Shield with your study, your 1967 paper and the cautions.
suggestions.advice_note: Approve. I put it with the glutamate tools because that's what your study is about; if you'd rather it sat by the Fog table, say so in your comment and I'll move it. Once you approve, I check it in Pangram before it goes in, as the new rule asks of every paragraph of mine.
